get.summary: GET /admin/remote-access/api/proxy/auth/
get.description:
nginx's `auth_request` target for the /sdlan-proxy/ location. It forwards
the original URI and the caller's cookies; everything this needs is in
those two.

204 = let it through, 403 = do not. Both are bare statuses with no body:
nginx discards an auth_request body anyway, so a JSON payload here would
only be bytes on every single proxied asset.

Session cookie only, and the anonymous case is answered here rather than by
IsAuthenticated. Two reasons, both about what the BROWSER ends up seeing —
nginx passes a 401 or 403 from the subrequest straight through to it:

  * DRF's default authenticators attach `WWW-Authenticate` and answer 401,
    which makes a browser raise a credentials prompt on what is supposed to
    be an invisible check. Verified against the running API: an anonymous
    caller got 401, not 403.
  * Anything outside 2xx/401/403 is a server error to nginx, so a redirect
    to the login page would surface as a 500 on the endpoint the operator
    was trying to open.

post.summary: POST /admin/remote-access/api/proxy/close/<session_id>/
post.description:
Revokes the window immediately instead of letting it lapse. 404 when the id
is unknown, already closed, or belongs to somebody else — all three are the
same answer from the caller's side: there is nothing here to close.
POST /admin/remote-access/api/proxy/open/

get.summary: GET /admin/remote-access/api/tunnel/auth/
get.description:
nginx's `auth_request` target for the public tunnel ports in
deploy/nginx/sdlan-tunnel.conf. nginx sends the port it was listening on as
`X-Original-Port` and forwards the caller's cookies; that is everything
this needs.

204 = let it through, 403 = do not. Bare statuses with no body, because
nginx discards an auth_request body and this runs on every single asset the
proxied page pulls.

On 204 it also answers `X-Tunnel-Upstream`, which nginx lifts into the
upstream URL with `auth_request_set`. The scheme has to come from here: the
far end of a tunnel is free to speak either, the port cannot be read as a
hint (ttyd serves TLS on 8015), and nginx has no way to look up the row.
That keeps ONE server block per port instead of one per port per scheme.

Session cookie only, and the anonymous case is answered here rather than by
IsAuthenticated — for the same two reasons ProxyAuthView documents: DRF's
default authenticators would answer 401 with `WWW-Authenticate` and raise a
browser credentials prompt on an invisible check, and anything outside
2xx/401/403 reaches the operator as a 500 on the page they were opening.

post.description:
Admin action: turn OFF two-factor for another user — e.g. when they have
lost their device. Removes their TOTP and backup devices.

If the target still has `require_2fa` set they will be sent back through
setup on next sign-in — this is a reset, not an exemption. To exempt them, an
admin also unticks "Require two-factor authentication".

get.description: Hand the SPA a CSRF token to send on subsequent writes.

Current user + setup state — the SPA reads this on load/refresh to decide
where to send the user (dashboard vs /setup). A 403 tells the SPA to show the
login page.

A session that has passed the password step but NOT the 2FA token step is
only half-authenticated: the login view creates it (so `verify` can complete
it) but it must not count as signed-in for the app. django-otp exposes this
as `user.is_verified()` — a user with a device who has not verified fails it.
Treat that as "not logged in" so the SPA keeps showing the token step rather
than falling through to the dashboard.

post.summary: Send a password-reset email for the given address.
post.description:
Uses ALLAUTH's ResetPasswordForm, not Django's — this project's reset-confirm
flow is allauth's (`account_reset_password_from_key`), so Django's form crashed
with NoReverseMatch trying to reverse `password_reset_confirm`. Allauth builds
the correct link + email its own confirm view expects.

Always answers 200 — never reveal whether an address is registered (an
enumeration leak). A send failure is logged, not surfaced, for the same
reason.

Set a new password from a valid reset link. Applies the configured
password validators (via allauth's ResetPasswordKeyForm) so weak passwords
are rejected with a readable message.

Check that a reset link is still valid, so the React page can show the
set-password form (or an "expired link" message) before the user types.

post.summary: Hand one stored backup to the operator as a file.
post.description:
``POST`` rather than ``GET`` because the encrypted format takes a
passphrase, and a passphrase in a query string ends up in the access log,
the browser history and any proxy in between.

Two formats, both of the same content — the verbatim UCI export the backup
was taken from:

  * ``plain``     — the text as stored, readable in any editor.
  * ``encrypted`` — the same text inside an ``openssl enc`` envelope keyed
    by the caller's passphrase (see :mod:`config_compare.crypto`).

Authorisation is stricter than the list endpoint on purpose: the list
withholds ``raw_uci_text`` precisely because it carries PSKs, WiFi keys and
user passwords, so downloading it requires being a manager of the owning
organization, not merely being logged in.

post.summary: Push one backup's stored configuration to many devices.
post.description:
The REST equivalent of the admin page's second tab. Note what this is NOT:
applying a backup is not attaching a template. A backup holds the verbatim
UCI text pulled off a device, so it cannot be attached — it is pushed over
SSH, through the same PushedConfig + push_device_config path the Config
Compare screen uses. That is why the response says queued and points at
Pushed Config for progress.

Destructive by nature: it overwrites the running configuration of every
selected device with a snapshot taken from (usually) a different one. The
org and manager checks below are the same as bulk apply-template's; the
caller is expected to confirm intent before getting here.

post.summary: Apply templates to many devices at once.
post.description:
The REST equivalent of the admin's bulk-apply-template page, which the
React device list previously had no way to reach. Same rules as that view,
restated here rather than imported because it is a TemplateResponse flow
tangled up with forms and redirects:

  * every selected device must be in ONE organization — templates are
    org-scoped, so a mixed selection has no single valid template list
  * the caller must manage that organization (superusers excepted)
  * a device with no Config gets one, otherwise there is nothing to
    attach templates to
  * mode 'add' unions with what is already applied, 'replace' sets

Wrapped in a transaction: a partial apply across a fleet is worse than a
clean failure, because you cannot tell by looking which half took.

post.summary: Queue an on-demand config snapshot for each selected device.
post.description:
The REST equivalent of config_compare's "Create config backup (snapshot
now)" admin action, and it calls the very same Celery task, so the two
routes cannot drift.

Queues rather than snapshots: the task SSHes to the device. It also skips
writing a duplicate when nothing changed since the last backup, which is
why the response says "queued" and not "created".

        option ip_end <ipv4>

        option mru <int>
        option username <str>
        option password <str>
        option lcp_interval <int>

        option require_mschap_v2 '0'|'1'

        option require_pap '0'|'1'

get.summary:
Aggregate Control Plane (VPN server) count + reachability for the
**Control Plane** card on the dashboard Overview tab.
get.description:
"Control Plane" is the operator-facing name for ``config.Vpn`` servers
(admin at ``/admin/config/vpn/``). The VPN model has no online/offline
field, so reachability is derived the same way the VPN-uptime report does:
match each VPN ``host`` to a managed Device (by ``management_ip`` /
``last_ip``) and treat the server as *online* when that device's monitoring
status is ``ok``. A VPN whose host matches no monitored device — or matches
a device that is not ``ok`` — counts as *offline* (reachability unconfirmed).

Response shape::

    {"total": 3, "online": 2, "offline": 1, "as_of": "2026-06-04T..Z"}

Aggregate counts only — never VPN names, hosts, or device IDs. Org-scoped:
non-superusers only ever count VPNs in their own organizations.

get.summary: Aggregate Inbound/Outbound Mbps distribution across all org WAN interfaces.
get.description:
Powers the **Interface Throughput** card (Inbound + Outbound doughnuts) on
the WAN Uplinks dashboard tab.

Query params (forwarded to :func:`get_data_usage_payload_for_request`):
  * ``period`` — ``1d`` (default) | ``3d`` | ``7d`` | ``30d`` | ``365d``
  * ``location_id``, ``floorplan_id``, ``ifname`` — optional filters
  * ``nocache=1`` to bypass the 60s cache (debugging only)

Response shape::

    {
      "inbound":  [{"bucket": "<100", "count": 12}, ...],   # rx-direction
      "outbound": [{"bucket": "<100", "count": 8},  ...],   # tx-direction
      "total_interfaces": 16,
      "as_of": "2026-05-08T10:30:00Z"
    }

The four buckets are always present in the same order:
``<100 / 100-500 / 500-1000 / >1000`` (Mbps).

Aggregate SD-WAN overlay (NsBondTopology) count + status for the
**SD-WAN Overlays** card on the dashboard Overview tab.

Each :class:`NsBondTopology` is one overlay fabric. Counts are grouped by
the topology ``status`` state machine into three pills:

* ``deployed`` — status ``deployed``
* ``error``    — status ``error`` / ``failed``
* ``pending``  — everything else (draft / computed / validated / deploying /
  undeploying)

Response shape::

    {"total": 5, "deployed": 3, "pending": 1, "error": 1, "as_of": "..Z"}

Aggregate counts only. Org-scoped exactly like the nsbond map-tunnels view.
